blocks.text: **Devmaxx topic:** Microservices. **Goal:** decide where the boundaries go — and often, decide not to split.

sections.title: 1. The honest case for and against

blocks.text: For

rows: Only if the teams and pipelines are genuinely independent
Only if the components have different scaling profiles
Real, but costly (each service = a new hiring/on-call surface)
Real, if the boundaries match the failure domains

blocks.text: Against

rows: Every call is a potential partial failure
You need sagas, idempotency, and reconciliation
You need tracing, correlation IDs, and good tooling
Every service needs deploys, monitoring, on-call, runbooks
Contract tests, test environments, integration suites
Network hops add up (and p99 stacks)
Denormalization becomes necessary, consistency becomes your problem

blocks.text: **The honest summary:** microservices trade a *code* problem for an *operations* problem. That's a good trade at 50+ teams and a terrible one at 5. Most systems should start as a **modular monolith**.
**One deployable unit, with strict internal module boundaries.**
**How to keep the boundaries real:**

items.text: **Separate schema per module** (Postgres schemas, separate databases) — enforced by permissions, so one module can't query another's tables.
**Modules communicate via in-process interfaces**, not direct table access.
**CI checks**: a dependency-cruiser-style rule that forbids module A from importing module B directly.
**Separate tables per module even in one DB** — no cross-module joins at runtime.

blocks.text: **Why this is good:** you get the *organizational* benefits of clear boundaries without the distributed-systems tax. And when you later extract a service, you already have the seam.
**When to split out of a monolith:**

items.text: The component needs a **different scaling profile** (media transcoding vs. API traffic).
It has a **different release cadence** or language/runtime.
It has a **different security/ownership boundary**.
A team needs **independent deploys** (and the team is large enough).
The component is a **performance bottleneck** that pollutes the main process.
It's a **large team** (>15) — beyond that, a single codebase becomes a coordination bottleneck.

blocks.text: Bounded Context (Domain-Driven Design)
The core idea: a business domain has subdomains, and each subdomain is a **bounded context** with its own ubiquitous language, model, and rules.

blocks.code:
Subdomain: Commerce
  Bounded Context: Orders      (Order, LineItem, Fulfillment)
  Bounded Context: Catalog     (Product, Variant, Pricing)
  Bounded Context: Payments    (Payment, Charge, Refund)
  Bounded Context: Inventory   (Stock, Reservation, Warehouse)

blocks.text: **Within a bounded context**, the model is consistent and the language is shared. **Across contexts**, you integrate through explicit contracts (APIs, events), and the models may differ —that's not a bug, that's the point.
Signals you've drawn the boundary wrong

rows: **Chatty communication** (A calls B for every operation)
The boundary is too fine, or the operation isn't atomic
The boundary splits a single business transaction

blocks.text: Heuristics for good boundaries

items.text: **Align with business capabilities**, not technical layers. ("Customers", "Orders", "Billing") not ("Controllers", "Services", "Repositories").
**High cohesion, low coupling** — a change to one service shouldn't ripple.
**Own the data.** A service owns its tables; nobody else reads them directly. Cross-domain reads go through the API or a published event.
**Prefer fewer, larger services** at the start. Splitting is easy; merging is hard.
**A service should be runnable and useful alone** (except for a few foundational ones like auth).
**If the same two services always change together, merge them.**

blocks.text: The "shared database" antipattern
Two services reading each other's tables have no boundary — you just added network latency to a join. If you must share, share via an API or a published event with a well-defined contract.
Synchronous (request/response)

rows: A gateway aggregating many services for a client that needs flexibility

blocks.text: **Rules for sync calls:**

items.text: **Set a deadline/timeout on every call** and propagate it.
**Use a circuit breaker** on every dependency.
**Make calls idempotent** so retries are safe.
**Limit fan-out** (a request calling 10 services serially = 10x latency). Parallelize and cap.
**Avoid N+1 across services** — fetch in batches.
**Use bulkheads** so one dependency can't exhaust your pool.

blocks.text: Asynchronous (events)

rows: High-throughput event streams, many consumers, replay

blocks.text: **Rules for async:**

items.text: Events are **facts about things that happened**, named in the past tense

blocks.text: (`OrderPlaced`, `PaymentCaptured`) — not commands (`ProcessOrder`).

items.text: **The producer doesn't know the consumers** — that's the point. New consumers can be added

blocks.text: without touching the producer.

items.text: **Version your event schemas**; consumers must tolerate unknown fields.
**Idempotent consumers** (Ch. 07).

blocks.text: Which one to choose

rows: Does the caller need the result immediately?
Does the caller need to retry on failure?
Is it a query (read) across domains?
Is it a state change that others may care about?

blocks.text: **The "notification vs. command" distinction:**

items.text: **Notification** ("OrderPlaced happened") → subscribers decide what to do. Loose coupling.
**Command** ("ShipOrder now") → one specific handler. Direct coupling, explicit.

blocks.text: The core rule
**Each service owns its data. No service reads another service's database.**

blocks.code:
Orders service ──┐
Payments service ─┼── each owns its store
Catalog service ─┘

blocks.text: **How services read each other's data:**
Data duplication is normal
Because services own their data, the same fact appears in several places (the order total in Orders, in the invoice, in the analytics pipeline). This is **intentional and managed**:

items.text: Each copy has a defined owner and a refresh mechanism.
Reconciliation jobs detect divergence.
The authoritative copy is documented.

blocks.text: Distributed transactions
Cross-service workflows use **sagas** (Ch. 05, Ch. 08):

items.text: Orchestrated (a saga manager drives it) — recommended for anything non-trivial.
Each step is a local transaction with a compensating action.
Compensations are forward operations, idempotent and retryable.
The saga state is durable so it can resume.

blocks.text: The outbox pattern
The standard way to publish reliably (Ch. 05, Ch. 07):

blocks.code:
Service transaction: write business row + write outbox row
Relay: read outbox → publish to broker → mark published
Consumer: idempotent processing

blocks.text: **Alternative: change data capture (CDC)** — read the DB's replication log (Debezium) and publish changes. No schema change to the app, and it captures changes from *any* code path (including direct SQL). It also captures data you might not want to publish (PII) — so filter carefully.

sections.title: 6. API gateway, BFF, and the edge

rows: Single entry point: routing, auth, rate limiting, aggregation
A gateway *per* client type (web, mobile, partner) tailored to that client's needs
Sidecar proxies handling mTLS, retries, timeouts, telemetry, traffic policies
CDN + edge compute for static and globally cached content

blocks.text: **Benefits of a gateway:** one place for cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting, quotas, logging, protocol translation); hides internal topology from clients; enables protocol translation (gRPC ↔ REST).

**Costs:** the gateway is a critical path component (needs HA, and its latency adds to every request); it can become a monolith of business logic (resist this — the gateway should be thin); it's a coupling point for every team.

**Service mesh (Envoy, Istio, Linkerd):** moves service-to-service concerns (mTLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, telemetry) out of the app code into a proxy. Pros: consistency, language-agnostic, no code changes. Cons: significant complexity, a new layer to debug, resource overhead. For a handful of services, a mesh is overkill.
**Best practice:** rolling deploys + canary for the risky parts + feature flags for fast mitigation + **automatic rollback** on a burn-rate alert.
Database changes with microservices
**Expand-and-contract** (Ch. 09):

items.text: Add the new column/table (backward compatible).
Deploy code that writes both, reads the new one.
Backfill.
Deploy code that reads only the new one.
Drop the old column (a later release).

blocks.text: **Never** make a deploy that requires a schema change and a code change to land simultaneously.

rows: One service with its dependencies stubbed
The provider's API matches what consumers expect

blocks.text: **Consumer-driven contracts (Pact):** the consumer declares what it expects; the provider's CI verifies it still satisfies those expectations. This catches breaking changes *before* deployment — the single most valuable test type in a microservices setup.
**The "test pyramid in microservices"**: many unit tests, many contract tests, fewer integration tests, few E2E tests, plus continuous chaos testing in staging.
**Test environment strategy:**

items.text: **Shared staging** (one environment, all services) — simplest, but flaky and slow.
**Per-PR environments** (ephemeral, spun up per branch) — modern best practice (Kubernetes +

blocks.text: GitOps).

items.text: **Production traffic replay** (shadow traffic) — catches what your tests missed.

blocks.text: **Every request carries a trace context** (Ch. 14). Without it, a distributed system is unknowable.
Minimum for each service:

items.text: **RED metrics** (rate, errors, duration) per route.
**Distributed tracing** with automatic context propagation.
**Structured logs** with `trace_id`.
**Health/readiness endpoints.**
**Dependency dashboards** (DB, cache, broker latency and errors).
**An owner** (team, in the metadata, on the dashboard).

blocks.text: **The golden signals must be per service AND aggregated.** "The checkout service's error rate" is actionable; "the platform's error rate" is not.

rows: Services that must deploy together, with chatty sync calls
No real boundary; corrupted by any team's change
Own the data; integrate via API/events
Latency stacks; a slow hop fails everything
Distributed-system tax before the scale justifies it

items.text: **Modularize a monolith.** Take a small app with three features. Give each module its own tables, define interfaces between modules, add a CI check that forbids cross-module table access and direct imports, and verify the app still works. Now you have extraction seams.

**Extract one service.** Choose a module with a different scaling profile. Extract it behind an API, replace the in-process call with an HTTP/gRPC call, and add: timeouts, a circuit breaker, retries with idempotency, and a contract test. Measure the added latency.
**Contract test.** Use Pact (or a hand-rolled version): the consumer declares the expectations; change the provider's response shape; verify the provider's CI fails.

**Saga with compensation.** Order → Payment → Shipment with a durable saga orchestrator. Inject failures at each step; verify the compensations restore consistency and that a crash mid-saga resumes correctly.
**Ownership map.** For every service, write down: the owning team, the on-call rotation, the runbook, the SLO, and the dashboard. If a service has no named owner, that's the finding.

blocks.text: Good: "I'd start as a modular monolith with clean boundaries — separate schemas per domain, communication through interfaces, CI checks enforcing it. That's faster to build and still lets us extract services later. The extraction triggers would be: the transcoding service needs independent scaling, or a team grows large enough to need independent deploys."

Better: "For the payments context I'd extract a service because it has a different compliance boundary and a different release cadence. It would own its data, publish `PaymentCaptured` events via the transactional outbox, and be called synchronously only for the authorization check. Every call has a deadline, a circuit breaker, and idempotency keys; contract tests protect the interface."
Red flags: "we'll split it into microservices because it scales better" with no boundary reasoning; shared databases; chatty service calls; no mention of distributed transactions.

selfCheck.q: **What is a modular monolith, and why is it often the right starting point?**
selfCheck.a: A single deployable unit with strict internal module boundaries (separate schemas, enforced interfaces, CI checks). You get clear ownership and extraction seams without the network, transaction, and operational complexity of distributed services. It's also much faster to build and debug.

selfCheck.q: **What is a bounded context?**
selfCheck.a: A DDD concept: a sub-part of the domain with its own model, rules, and language, within which the model is consistent. Services should map to bounded contexts, not to database tables or technical layers.

selfCheck.q: **Give three signs your service boundaries are in the wrong place.**
selfCheck.a: (a) Services are chatty — many network calls per user request. (b) You need distributed transactions across them, meaning the boundary splits a single business operation. (c) They share tables, so the boundary isn't real. (d) They always change together (should be one service).

selfCheck.q: **Why should each service own its data exclusively?**
selfCheck.a: Because direct database access has no contract, no isolation, and no enforcement — it's a hidden API that breaks silently. Owning the data makes the boundary enforceable (permissions, schemas) and lets the service change its internals without coordinating.

selfCheck.q: **What's the difference between a notification event and a command?**
selfCheck.a: A **notification** announces a fact ("OrderPlaced happened") and leaves it to subscribers to decide what to do — loose coupling, many consumers. A **command** asks for a specific action ("ShipOrder now") with one intended handler — explicit coupling.

selfCheck.q: **When should you use async messaging instead of a sync call?**
selfCheck.a: When the caller doesn't need the result immediately, when there are multiple independent consumers, when work should be retried reliably, or when a slow dependency shouldn't block the user. Async decouples availability and timing.

selfCheck.q: **What is the outbox pattern, and what problem does it solve in a microservices context?**
selfCheck.a: It guarantees that a state change in the service and the publication of the corresponding event happen together (one local transaction with an outbox row), eliminating the dual-write failure. A relay publishes the events, and consumers are idempotent.

selfCheck.q: **What is CDC and how does it differ from the outbox pattern?**
selfCheck.a: **CDC** reads the database's replication log and publishes every change, without the app writing anything special. It's app-agnostic (captures changes from any code path) but requires filtering (you may publish PII) and couples to your DB schema.

selfCheck.q: **What is a saga, and what property does it give up vs. a distributed transaction?**
selfCheck.a: A saga is a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions. Compared to 2PC it gives up **atomicity** (no all-or-nothing moment; intermediate states are visible) and **isolation**, in exchange for no blocking and no coordinator dependency.

selfCheck.q: **What is a BFF and how does it differ from a general API gateway?**
selfCheck.a: A general API gateway handles cross-cutting concerns for all clients. A **BFF** is a gateway per client type, tailored to that client's needs (different response shapes, aggregation levels, and release cadence for web vs. mobile).

selfCheck.q: **What does a service mesh actually do, and when is it overkill?**
selfCheck.a: A mesh (Envoy/Istio/Linkerd) puts a proxy sidecar next to each service to handle mTLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, and telemetry — so those policies are consistent and language-agnostic. It's overkill for a handful of services; the complexity of debugging a proxy layer isn't worth it until you have enough services to need consistency.

selfCheck.q: **What is consumer-driven contract testing and why is it valuable?**
selfCheck.a: The consumer declares the API behavior it depends on; the provider's CI verifies it still satisfies those expectations. It catches breaking changes *before* they reach production, which is the main cause of cross-service coordination pain.

selfCheck.q: **What is expand-and-contract and why can't you change a schema and code at once?**
selfCheck.a: Because an old code version and a new schema version coexist during a rolling deploy. If the new code requires the new column and the migration hasn't run yet, it breaks; if the migration removes the old column and old instances still read it, it breaks. Expand-and-contract guarantees both versions work at every step.

selfCheck.q: **What is a "distributed monolith"?**
selfCheck.a: A set of services that are deployed together, depend on each other synchronously, and share data — all the costs of microservices with none of the benefits. It's usually microservices split along technical layers rather than business capabilities.

selfCheck.q: **What is a "god service" and why does it happen?**
selfCheck.a: Because a service grew organically until it handled every use case, or because nobody made a boundary decision and everything defaulted to the one existing service. Fix: identify the business capabilities inside it and split along those.

selfCheck.q: **When is splitting a service the wrong move?**
selfCheck.a: When the components always change together, when the data must be transactionally consistent across them, when the team is small (the operational overhead exceeds the benefit), or when the required independence (scaling, release, security) doesn't actually exist.

selfCheck.q: **What are the four things every cross-service call needs?**
selfCheck.a: **A timeout/deadline**, **a circuit breaker**, **idempotency** (so retries are safe), and **retries with backoff and jitter** (only for idempotent operations). Plus: a bulkhead so the dependency can't exhaust your pool, and a metric so you know it's failing.

selfCheck.q: **Why is data duplication between services acceptable?**
selfCheck.a: Because each service owns its data, and other services legitimately need a copy for their own decisions (the invoice needs the order total). With a clear owner, a defined refresh mechanism, and reconciliation to detect divergence, duplication is a managed, intentional trade-off for independence.

selfCheck.q: **What is a golden signal and what should it be measured per service?**
selfCheck.a: The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. Measured per service and per route, because "checkout's p99 is high" is actionable while "the platform's p99 is high" is not.

selfCheck.q: **What is the relationship between Conway's Law and service boundaries?**
selfCheck.a: Conway's Law says organizations produce systems that mirror their communication structures. So if teams communicate a lot across a boundary, the boundary is probably wrong (or the communication should change). Conversely, designing boundaries that match how teams want to work tends to produce systems that are easier to change.
